Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: acute chest tightness for ~3 hours with mild shortness of breath.
- Associated symptoms: wheeze, non-productive cough persisting after a recent cold last week; prior sore throat and runny nose that have improved; symptoms worse with exertion (stairs), not short of breath at rest.
- Onset/duration/progression: chest tightness began approximately 3 hours prior to consultation; cough persisted from recent cold.
- Past medical history:
  - Asthma (since childhood).
  - Hay fever and environmental allergies (dust).
  - Childhood eczema.
  - Childhood milk protein allergy.
  - History of severe asthma exacerbation requiring hospitalization and intubation at age ~16–17.
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol (Ventolin) — dose/route/frequency not documented; patient reports he has run out and does not have it with him now.
  - Clenil Modulite (inhaled steroid) — dose/route/frequency not documented; patient reports he has run out and does not have it with him now.
  - Patient reported having run out of inhalers about one week ago.
- Social history:
  - Student (away at university recently); no other social history documented.
- Allergies:
  - No drug allergies reported.

Objective:
- Physical examination: none documented in transcript.
  - No vital signs provided.
  - No peak flow or oxygen saturation available.
- Investigations: none performed or planned during consultation (no results documented).

Assessment & Plan:

1. Asthma exacerbation:
   - Assessment/likely diagnosis: Asthma exacerbation
   - Differential diagnosis:
     - Viral bronchospasm/post-infectious wheeze
     - Other causes of chest tightness/wheeze (not further explored in transcript)
   - Investigations planned: none documented
   - Treatment planned:
     - Prescription for inhaled short-acting bronchodilator (Salbutamol/Ventolin) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
     - Prescription for inhaled corticosteroid (Clenil Modulite) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
     - Oral corticosteroid tablets prescribed for 5 days: two tablets in the morning (specific corticosteroid name not documented).
     - Spacer device to be provided with instructions on use.
     - Inhaler use plan: continue Clenil daily; use Ventolin as needed (PRN).
     - Safety advice: seek medical attention if Ventolin required more frequently than every 3 hours or if symptoms worsen (increased shortness of breath, chest pain/tightness, light-headedness).
   - Relevant referrals: none documented

2. Recent/ongoing upper respiratory tract infection (post-viral cough):
   - Assessment/likely diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory tract infection/post-infectious cough
   - Differential diagnosis:
     - Asthma-related cough/wheeze triggered by viral infection
   - Investigations planned: none documented
   - Treatment planned:
     - Supportive care; management focused on asthma control as above.
   - Relevant referrals: none documented
